Accessibility facts about the emoji in a text column

Source: R/emoji-access.R
emoji_a11y_check.Rd

emoji_a11y_check() reports, per row, the facts the accessibility taxonomy of Griggio, Gorman and Tigwell (CSCW 2024) is built from: how often an emoji or a sequence repeats, where emoji sit, which are ambiguous or carry long modified names, and how many characters a screen reader would say for them. It reports facts and gives no verdicts: whether a message is too much is the writer's call, which is the paper's own finding.

Usage

emoji_a11y_check(data, text, max_name = 40L, presentation = "emoji")

Arguments

data

A data frame or tibble containing a text column. Grouped data frames are accepted. The verbs that work a row at a time (adding columns, or keeping and expanding rows) carry the grouping through to their result, as dplyr::mutate() and dplyr::filter() do. The verbs that pool across rows – the counts, the co-occurrence edge lists, the time series – warn that they ignore the grouping and return one corpus-wide answer.

text

The text column to scan, supplied unquoted. Any atomic column is accepted and read as character, so a factor works and a numeric, Date or logical one simply contains no emoji. A list column – or a data-frame column – is refused rather than coerced, because coercing one deparses it and the emoji found would be in the code rather than in your data. What counts as an emoji is the same in every verb; see the Detection section of tidyEmoji for the one case that surprises people, code points that are emoji only when they carry U+FE0F.

max_name

A name longer than this many characters counts in .emoji_n_long_names. Default 40.

presentation

Which code points count as emoji: "emoji" (the default) or "any".

  • "emoji" requires emoji presentation, so U+2764 U+FE0F is an emoji and the bare U+2764 is not. This is the default and it will stay the default: widening it would silently recount every corpus already analysed.

  • "any" also reads the text-presentation spellings Unicode lists for an emoji (the bare heart, U+263A, U+2714, a keycap without its selector), because several keyboards emit them. It never reads the copyright, registered and trade-mark signs (U+00A9, U+00AE, U+2122), which are typography far more often than they are emoji.

"any" only ever adds occurrences: everything "emoji" finds, it finds too, in the same place. emoji_coverage() reports how many it adds and how many of those a lexicon can score, which is the cost of the choice in one number. Every verb that counts, scores or rewrites the emoji in a text column takes this argument, so counts still agree across the package for whichever value you use. The flag verbs do not need it, since a flag has no text-presentation form.

Value

data, as a tibble, with added columns .emoji_max_repeat, .emoji_n_repeated_seqs, .emoji_longest_run, .emoji_n_mid, .emoji_n_begin, .emoji_n_ambiguous, .emoji_n_modifier_names (see Details), .emoji_spoken_chars (the characters of the row's emoji names), .emoji_n_char (the text's own length, the denominator; NA for NA text), .emoji_n_long_names (names longer than max_name), .emoji_n_ri_letters (regional indicators that spell no flag, which a screen reader reads out one letter at a time) and .emoji_n_hidden (hidden code points, as emoji_hidden() counts them). A grouped input stays grouped.

Details

The columns follow the taxonomy. Number of emoji: .emoji_max_repeat (1a, one emoji repeated), .emoji_n_repeated_seqs (1b, the same pair of different emoji written together more than once; a run of one emoji is 1a, not 1b) and .emoji_longest_run (1c, a run of emoji of any kind, as emoji_runs() segments it). Placement: .emoji_n_mid (2a, inside the text) and .emoji_n_begin (2b, opening it). The package does no sentence segmentation, so these are relative to the row; split your text into sentences first and they are exactly the paper's. Purpose: .emoji_n_ambiguous (3a, emoji in the top tenth of emoji_ambiguity()'s polarisation, which reads the bundled lexicon and so is 0 for the emoji it cannot score; emoji_coverage() says how many those are) and .emoji_n_modifier_names (3b, emoji whose name a skin tone or a gender extends, as in "woman facepalming: light skin tone").

The paper's Alert fired on one emoji three times, two emoji twice each, and three different emoji in a row. Those are thresholds to apply to these columns if you want them; the verb applies none. The design its participants preferred, a Preview of what a screen reader will say, is emoji_to_text() with format = "name".

Spoken length is a proxy. .emoji_spoken_chars adds up the CLDR names, which is what NVDA's symbol dictionaries are built from; VoiceOver, the Windows readers and TalkBack each announce their own strings, and Remy Sharp's emoji accessibility reference tabulates them. Some readers shorten a repeat ("three face with tears of joy"), which the column does not model. On the bundled sample, naming every emoji takes the emoji-bearing rows from 147,742 characters to 171,606, 16.2% more, and 50 of its 750 emoji-bearing rows hold a run of three or more.

max_name is the one threshold, because a long name is a property of the catalogue rather than of the text: four catalogue names in five are 40 characters or shorter (the median is 26), so the default flags 18.7% of the catalogue, but only 1 of the sample's 1,454 occurrences, because the emoji people use most have short names.

References

Griggio, C. F., Gorman, B. M. and Tigwell, G. W. (2024). "Party Face Congratulations!" Exploring design ideas to help sighted users with emoji accessibility when messaging with screen reader users. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 8 (CSCW1), article 175. doi:10.1145/3641014

See also

emoji_to_text() for the Preview; emoji_runs(); emoji_ambiguity().

Examples

d <- data.frame(text = c(
  "lol \U0001f602\U0001f602\U0001f602\U0001f602",
  "\U0001f389\u2764\ufe0f yes \U0001f389\u2764\ufe0f",
  "so \U0001f389 much fun"))
emoji_a11y_check(d, text)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 13
#>   text  .emoji_max_repeat .emoji_n_repeated_seqs .emoji_longest_run .emoji_n_mid
#>   <chr>             <int>                  <int>              <int>        <int>
#> 1 lol …                 4                      0                  4            0
#> 2 🎉❤️ y…                 2                      1                  2            0
#> 3 so 🎉…                 1                      0                  1            1
#> # ℹ 8 more variables: .emoji_n_begin <int>, .emoji_n_ambiguous <int>,
#> #   .emoji_n_modifier_names <int>, .emoji_spoken_chars <int>,
#> #   .emoji_n_char <int>, .emoji_n_long_names <int>, .emoji_n_ri_letters <int>,
#> #   .emoji_n_hidden <int>
